passages.t: The grace given to the churches of Macedonia
passages.happening:
Paul turns to the gift he has been gathering for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He begins with a story. “Now, brothers, we want you to know about the grace that God has given the churches of Macedonia” (verse 1).

The churches of Macedonia were in trouble, and they were poor. Yet something overflowed. “In the terrible ordeal they suffered, their abundant joy and deep poverty overflowed into rich generosity” (verse 2).

They gave as much as they could, and more. No one pushed them. “For I testify that they gave according to their ability and even beyond it. Of their own accord, they earnestly pleaded with us for the privilege of sharing in this service to the saints” (verses 3 and 4). They begged to be allowed to give.

Paul had not expected so much. He says that “they gave themselves first to the Lord and then to us, because it was the will of God” (verse 5).

So Paul asked Titus to help the Corinthians finish what they had begun (verse 6). They are rich in many gifts, he says, so “see that you also excel in this grace of giving” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Macedonia was the Roman province of northern Greece. Paul's churches there were in Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea (Acts 16 and 17). From the start those believers had suffered for their faith. Paul told the Thessalonians that they welcomed the message “in spite of your great suffering” (1 Thessalonians 1:6). The Philippians had sent money to Paul again and again (Philippians 4:15-16). Now, poor themselves, they wanted to help people they had never met.

Who were ‘the saints’ in Jerusalem? ‘Saints’ means God's holy people, all believers, not a special few. The church in Jerusalem had many poor members. Acts tells of a famine in the days of the emperor Claudius, when believers in Antioch sent help to Judea (Acts 11:28-30). When the leaders in Jerusalem agreed that Paul should preach to the Gentiles, “They only asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do” (Galatians 2:10).

For Paul the gift meant more than food. It joined Gentile churches to the Jewish church where the gospel began. He wrote to Rome, “For if the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual blessings, they are obligated to minister to them with material blessings” (Romans 15:27).

Listen to the word ‘grace’. In Greek it is charis. It means favour freely given, and from there a gift, a kindness, or thanks. It comes seven times in this chapter. Paul calls the Macedonians' giving ‘the grace that God has given’. Their generosity was God's work in them before it was their work.

In Corinth, a rich man's gift usually came with strings. A patron, a wealthy supporter, gave a building or a feast and received honour and loyalty in return. Paul never speaks of this gift in those terms. It is grace, service and sharing. The word in verse 4 translated ‘sharing’ is koinōnia, fellowship.
passages.ot:
Israel's law and prophets taught care for the poor as part of loving God. “Give generously to him, and do not let your heart be grieved when you do so” (Deuteronomy 15:10).

Willing giving goes back to the building of the tabernacle in the wilderness. God told Moses to receive an offering “from every man whose heart compels him” (Exodus 25:2). “Let everyone whose heart is willing bring an offering to the LORD” (Exodus 35:5).

When David gathered gifts for the temple, he said that giving was itself a gift from God. “But who am I, and who are my people, that we should be able to give as generously as this? For everything comes from You, and from Your own hand we have given to You” (1 Chronicles 29:14). That is close to what Paul says of Macedonia: the grace to give came from God.
passages.asks: The Macedonians gave out of deep poverty, and they begged to give. Ask what makes giving feel like a loss to you, and what would make it feel like a privilege. Paul says they gave themselves first to the Lord. Ask whether your money follows where your heart has already gone, or whether it is the one thing you have kept back.

passages.t: ‘Though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor’
passages.happening:
Paul is careful. “I am not making a demand, but I am testing the sincerity of your love in comparison to the earnestness of others” (verse 8).

Then he gives the real reason to give. It is not the Macedonians. It is Christ. “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich” (verse 9).

He gives his advice. The Corinthians were the first to start, a year ago. “Now finish the work, so that you may complete it just as eagerly as you began, according to your means” (verse 11). God does not ask for what a person does not have. “For if the eagerness is there, the gift is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what he does not have” (verse 12).

Paul does not want them crushed. “It is not our intention that others may be relieved while you are burdened, but that there may be equality” (verse 13). Today they have more and can help. Another day, it may be the other way round (verse 14).

He ends with Scripture: “He who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
‘He became poor’ is one word in Greek, ptōcheuō. It means to become a beggar, to be reduced to nothing. It comes only here in the New Testament. A Corinthian knew what it meant to rise in the world. Here is someone who went the other way on purpose.

When was Christ rich? Paul means before he was born as a man. He says the same in another letter: Christ, “existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness” (Philippians 2:6-7). He was born to a poor family. He said, “the Son of Man has no place to lay His head” (Matthew 8:20). And he went all the way to the cross.

‘That there may be equality’ uses the Greek word isotēs, which also means fairness. Paul does not say that everyone must own the same things. He says that what is spare in one place should meet what is lacking in another, so that no believer is crushed while another has plenty. And he expects the help to run both ways. Jerusalem had already given Corinth something greater: the gospel itself.

Some readers today use verses 13 to 15 to argue for one economic or political system, and others to argue against one. Paul is not writing about government or taxes. He is asking churches to share freely with other believers in need. These notes draw no political lesson from it, left or right.
passages.ot:
Verse 15 quotes the story of the manna, the bread God sent Israel in the wilderness. Each family was told to gather as much as it needed. “So the Israelites did this. Some gathered more, and some less. When they measured it by the omer, he who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall. Each one gathered as much as he needed to eat” (Exodus 16:17-18). Paul quotes the middle of that verse almost word for word.

In the wilderness, God made the sharing happen. No one could hoard manna; what was kept overnight rotted (Exodus 16:20). Paul's point is that God's people should now share by choice, so that the same thing comes true among them.

Behind 8:9 stands the long story of God coming down to his people. Isaiah speaks of the Servant who “poured out His life unto death” (Isaiah 53:12). And the Psalms say again and again that God hears the poor: “This poor man called out, and the LORD heard him” (Psalm 34:6).
passages.hard:
What does 8:9 say about Christ, and what does it promise?

It says something very great about Jesus. Christ was rich before he became poor. That means he was alive before he was born in Bethlehem. The church confesses this plainly, in the words of the Nicene Creed: the Son ‘for us men and for our salvation came down from heaven’, and ‘was made man’. He did not begin to exist at his birth. He came. This is part of the faith Christians everywhere confess, not one view among several.

What, then, are the riches he gives? They are not money. Paul has just praised the Macedonians, who stayed poor and gave anyway. He himself was often hungry (11:27). The riches are what Christ's coming and death won: forgiveness, a place in God's family, the Spirit, and a future with God. In his first letter Paul told the Corinthians, “For in Him you have been enriched in every way” (1 Corinthians 1:5). The riches he names there are gifts of God, “in all speech and all knowledge” (1 Corinthians 1:5).

So these notes say it plainly. ‘So that you through His poverty might become rich’ is not a promise that believers will have more money. Some teachers have used this verse to say that Jesus became poor so that Christians could be wealthy. That reading turns the verse upside down. Christ's poverty was not a payment to make us rich in goods. It was love that gave everything away, and Paul holds it up so that the Corinthians would do the same. The book page's part ‘What the letter is not’ says more, and the note on 9:6-11 takes this up again.
passages.asks: Paul does not order the Corinthians to give. He reminds them of Jesus. Ask what it would mean for your giving to start from what Christ has given you, rather than from guilt or from what others give. Then think about equality: who near you, or far away, is short of what you have spare?

passages.t: Titus and the brothers: care to do what is right
passages.happening:
Paul thanks God for Titus, who cares for the Corinthians as Paul does (verse 16). Titus is coming to them gladly, of his own choice (verse 17).

With him Paul sends “the brother who is praised by all the churches for his work in the gospel” (verse 18). This man was “chosen by the churches to accompany us with the offering” (verse 19).

Paul explains why he is so careful. “We hope to avoid any criticism of the way we administer this generous gift. For we are taking great care to do what is right, not only in the eyes of the Lord, but also in the eyes of men” (verses 20 and 21).

A third man goes too, “our brother whose earnestness has been proven many times and in many ways” (verse 22). Paul gives each one his title: Titus his partner, the others “messengers of the churches, to the glory of Christ” (verse 23).

So, he says, show these men your love, in front of all the churches (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Paul does not name the two brothers. Many guesses have been made, but no one knows who they were. What matters to Paul is who chose them. One was chosen by the churches, not by Paul. That was the point.

Money carried a long way invited suspicion. Travelling teachers in the Greek world were often accused of being in it for profit. Paul had refused to take money from Corinth for himself (11:7-9), and still some said he was crafty (12:16). So he made sure he was never alone with the gift. Several trusted people would carry it, and some of them were picked by the givers.

‘The messengers of the churches’ is, word for word, ‘apostles of the churches’. Here the word does not mean one of the Twelve or Paul. It means a sent person, a delegate the churches trusted with a task.

Paul's care says something to churches today. Money given to God's work should be handled in the open. More than one trusted person should count it and keep the records. Givers should be able to see where it went. Paul did not say, ‘Trust me, I am an apostle.’ He arranged things so that no one had to. That is not lack of faith. It is honesty and love for the people who gave. These notes are not financial or legal advice, but the principle is plain in this passage.
passages.ot:
Verse 21 echoes Proverbs 3:4. The BSB, following the Hebrew, reads, “Then you will find favor and high regard in the sight of God and man” (Proverbs 3:4). The old Greek translation of that verse speaks of taking thought for what is good ‘in the sight of the Lord and of men’, and Paul's words are close to that form.

The Old Testament has its own picture of honest handling of gifts. When King Joash repaired the temple, two men counted the gifts together, a royal officer and a priest: “the royal scribe and the high priest would go up, count the money brought into the house of the LORD, and tie it up in bags” (2 Kings 12:10). Samuel at the end of his life asked the people, “Whose ox or donkey have I taken? Whom have I cheated or oppressed?” (1 Samuel 12:3). A leader's hands were meant to be clean.
passages.asks: Paul thought it worth great effort to be above suspicion with money. Ask how money is handled in the groups you belong to, and whether you would be glad for anyone to see how you handle what is entrusted to you. Ask too whether you can trust others with a task, as Paul trusted these brothers, and honour them for it.
